blocks.text: Welcome to the Category guide for Axiom of Choice, a manual for those who are thrilled to test speed, rigour and understanding of core Mathematical fundamentals.

Following the fair draw, delegates will directly jump into the battle field where two teams face off in a fast paced PVP match. With strategies it's all about staying light on your feet, spotting quick patterns and trusting your problem - solving instincts.
The Format: Three simultaneous 1 v 1 duels. The team with the higher score combined from all three duels will eventually move forward.
Bring your own mobile devices or laptops with a stable mobile data connection.
Make sure every team member has an active Matiks account ready to go.
Considering the matches will take place simultaneously, each team needs at least 3 seperate devices logged in and ready.
Quick mental estimation and pattent spotting.
Thinking on your feet when clock is ticking.
Intuitive puzzle navigation over heavy calculations.

Time to put your strategic minds together! Round 2 is a 90-minute puzzle-solving climb across 5 distinct ranks. Imagine it as navigating an interactive obstacle course of brain teasers, logical hurdles and lateral thinking problems. To make the battleground heated, mystery bombs are dropped every 30 minutes. The top 10 teams who conquer the most ground move on to the finals!

Team Cap: 1-3 Delegates The Format: Neatly circled questions will be checked, no marks for the solution but in case any team is found cheating, they can be double checked with their solution to maintain fairness.
Carry your own calculator with you, you will be provided with pen and paper (it's preferable to have stationery with you as well)
Spotting hidden geometrics, symmetry, and grid-based patterns without needing formulas.
Untangling tricky word puzzles, sequence riddles, and constraint games using pure reasoning.
Figuring out how moving parts, counters, or sequences behave when rules shift.

The Endstufe!! Now teams working is translated from solving puzzled maths to explaining core concepts of how the fundamentals work. Your team will pick an intriguing statement, dive into its core logic, and pitch a creative, well-researched defense to the jury. Whether you use slides, a quick video, or draw it out live on a board, this round is all about storytelling through logic and clear visual reasoning.
The Format: A live explaination of claims, proving each word said using mathematical ideas and logic in mere 5 minutes.

The Bonus Challenge: Teams scoring over 65% on their main defense unlock an extra point oppertunity. Teams will be given 3 minutes to determine a statement and prove your reasoning without any preparation time.

Bring with you your presentation or video working smoothly on at least 2 devices to avoid inconvenience. Make sure to carry a tab if you want to present live on it, else you will be provided with a board and marker (You need to inform the median beforehand)
Carry with you printed research if you want to present it to jury external of the 5 minutes presentation, neat A4 size sheets are recommended to maintain decorum for maths.
Breaking down big ideas into simple, beautiful explanations.
Drawing clear diagrams and visual proofs that instantly make sense to an audience.
Collaborating smoothly under pressure to defend your team's reasoning.

In this challenge, teams will be tasked with designing and constructing a protective structure that allows an egg to survive a drop from a designated height. Teams will be provided with a fixed selection of materials and a limited amount of time to design, build, and test their structures.

The objective is not only to protect the egg, but to develop an efficient engineering solution while working within the given material and time constraints. Teams will be expected to consider factors such as impact force, energy absorption, structural stability, weight distribution, and material selection when designing their structures.

During the challenge, teams will be subjected to undisclosed distractions and additional conditions introduced by the organizers. These may require teams to adapt their designs or respond to unexpected changes during the challenge. The exact nature of these distractions will not be revealed beforehand, requiring teams to account for uncertainty and demonstrate adaptability.

Teams will be evaluated based on the survival of the egg, structural performance, efficient use of materials, quality of engineering design, and their ability to adapt to unexpected conditions. Additional points may be awarded for particularly innovative or well-engineered solutions.

The challenge is designed to test engineering design, problem-solving, resource management, adaptability, and teamwork, while encouraging teams to develop solutions that remain effective even when faced with unforeseen circumstances.
And a surprise at the end…

In the Final Round, delegates will be presented with a realworld engineering problem at the beginning of the round. Each team will be given a fixed period of time to research the problem, analyze the available information, and develop a practical and innovative solution.

During the preparation period, teams will be expected to conduct research using reliable sources, identify the key challenges, analyze relevant data, perform necessary calculations, and support their proposed solution with sound engineering principles. Teams may use appropriate research tools and resources permitted by the organizers.

Following the preparation period, each team will present its findings and proposed solution to the judges and participating teams. Presentations should clearly explain the problem, research conducted, relevant data, engineering reasoning, proposed solution, advantages, limitations, and potential risks.

Teams will be evaluated on their understanding of the problem, quality and reliability of research, engineering analysis, use of data and calculations, practicality and creativity of their solution, clarity of presentation, and ability to defend their proposal under questioning.

The round is designed to simulate real-world engineering decision-making, where problems rarely have a single perfect answer. The strongest team will be the one that develops a well-researched, technically sound, practical solution and demonstrates the ability to justify and defend its decisions using evidence and logical reasoning.
A physics-related motion will be announced before the event through the event’s official platform/form and their side (opp/prop) will be told too.
They will then debate the motion in a structured format.
Qualifying teams will be given a new physics/sciencerelated issue at the event.
Teams will have limited preparation time to formulate their position.
The objective is not only to present arguments but to convince the room that their position is the most reasonable and scientifically sound.
At the end, participants/delegates will vote for the position they found most convincing.

Delegates take part in a fast-paced, interactive research and analytical assessment delivered on a digital testing platform. The round presents teams with unfamiliar scientific data, claims, and experimental models, requiring rapid evaluation of evidence, identification of methodological flaws, and deduction of valid conclusions under strict time constraints.

The assessment consists of 30 questions distributed across three difficulty tiers: 10 Easy, 10 Medium, and 10 Hard. Success requires balancing analytical rigor with rapid response times across data interpretation, experimental design, and source evaluation.
This is an elimination round. The top-performing teams advance to Round 2.
Assessment Format: Teams answer 30 timed questions — including multiple-choice, ordering, and data-entry formats — split evenly across three difficulty tiers (10 Easy, 10 Medium, 10 Hard).

Data & Visual Reasoning: Questions assess the ability to process and evaluate visual and tabular data, through data interpretation, graph analysis, graph selection, and experimental anomaly identification.

Critical Evaluation: Questions test the identification of flaws, confounding elements, and source validity, through error detection, source credibility evaluation, correlation vs. causation, and confounding variable analysis.
Scientific Investigation: Questions evaluate the core principles of structured scientific inquiry, through experimental design, research methodology selection, and hypothesis testing.
Evidence & Reasoning: Questions require synthesizing information to validate claims, through evidence matching, inference deduction, conclusion validity, and statistical reasoning.
Points awarded per correct answer against a predefined answer key; questions weighted by difficulty (Easy / Medium / Hard).
Response speed on the digital platform automatically calculates score bonuses. If written backup scoring is used, cumulative accuracy plus designated tie-breaker questions determine rank.
Analytical precision in data analysis, scientific rigor in experimental critique, and deductive logic under time pressure.

Delegates are given a controversial scientific theory or topic at the start of the round. The topic is not revealed beforehand, requiring delegates to quickly develop a scientifically backed and logically sound argument for why the theory is true or false.

Throughout the round, crisis updates are introduced that may either support or contradict the delegate's current position. These updates are treated as 100% factual and accurate. Delegates must critically assess the new information and, where necessary, revise their arguments within the given time limit.
This is an elimination round. The top-performing delegates advance to Round 3.
Topic Reveal: A controversial scientific theory or topic is revealed at the start of the round.
Initial Research: Delegates research the topic using credible sources and formulate an argument for why the theory is true or false.
Crisis Updates: New pieces of information are introduced throughout the round. Delegates must incorporate these updates into their research and reassess their position where necessary.
Final Submission: Delegates submit their revised research and final argument within the allocated time.
Ability to respond effectively to new information and revise their position.
Quality, credibility, and relevance of the evidence used.
Strength, consistency, and validity of the arguments presented.
DELEGATE CAP 3 to 4 delegates per team.

The final elimination stage of the Research category. Teams select a difficulty tier and are scored on how they approach and solve an experimental physics problem — not on how they organize themselves internally as a team.

Stage 1 — Tier Commitment: Teams pre-commit to a tier (Easy / Medium / Hard) before the round starts, not after seeing the problem. If a tier fills up, priority goes to teams with the stronger combined standing from Rounds 1–2. Once committed, there is no switching.

Stage 2 — Problem Reveal: Sealed problem cards are opened simultaneously across all stations, all tiers together, on the same start signal — regardless of tier. This keeps the round a genuine gamble rather than an easier ride on the same clock.

Stage 3 — Design & Execution Window: Every team, in every tier, works within the identical time window to design, run, and prepare their answer. Higher tiers pack more conceptual complexity and more open-ended design decisions into that same time window.

Stage 4 — Submission: Once the window closes, teams finalize a standardized write-up (setup/approach, data, calculation, final result, conclusion), keeping judging consistent no matter which tier a team ran.

Stage 5 — Judging: Judging takes place after the round has finished, not during it. Once every team has completed their experiment and prepared their answer, judges go team to team to evaluate approach, methodology, and result.

Scoring weighs reasoning and method heavily, not just whether the final result lands close to expected — this matters more at higher tiers, where the “right” approach is not obvious. Judging is scoped entirely to the team's problem-solving approach and execution, not to how tasks were divided internally.

Goldmann's Gambit puts participants at the frontier of the scientific discovery through a research-driven trading simulation. Teams trade stocks of 10-11 public limited companies within a fictional country, making strategic calls based on real-time updates grounded in real-world science.
Each team receives private login credentials - do not share with other teams.
Portfolios are accessed individually through the digital platform.
All trading activity is monitored and tracked.

10-11 public limited companies at the outset, each with a detailed backstory, R&D history, and current market position. New companies are introduced as the competition progresses, expanding the market with fresh listings.
Prices move on scientific breakthroughs, research setbacks, and industry developments modeled on real-world science.
Updates cover experimental results, funding rounds, regulatory decisions, and company news.
At least one new stock enters the market daily.
Fundamental Analysis - evaluating a company's scientific credibility and growth prospects.
Market interpretation - reading research updates and industry indicators.
Strategic Planning - diversification and risk management.
Real-time Adaption - responding quickly to breaking developments.
Capital Allocation - distributing funds across a growing list of companies.
Timing - spotting the right moment to buy or sell, especially around new listings.
Never share login credentials - results in immediate disqualification.
Maintain a stable internet connection throughout the competition.
Report technical issues to administrators immediately.
Balance risk and return across all available companies.
Adapt as new stocks enter the market and conditions shift.
Make decisions under time pressure following each update.
Weigh unproven new listings against established companies.
A comprehensive explanation document will follow the competition, covering the rationale behind each update, the realworld science behind it, and an analysis of winning strategies.
Winner: The team with the highest asset value at the end of the competition .
Asset Calculation: Total Assets = Cash + (Shares × Final stock Price), summed across all companies.

Someone has been unalived. Five suspects remain. Six weapons. Three crime scenes. And the truth is buried beneath a web of lies. Welcome to The Last Sin, where every alibi can be broken, every clue can deceive, and every answer leads you closer to the killer, or deeper into the trap. Inspired by Cluedo, teams must investigate, decode, and reconstruct a crime designed to mislead. Use your critical thinking and sharpen your observation: some clues lie between the lines, while others hide in plain sight. Follow the evidence, question every detail, and uncover the truth before someone else does.

Three rooms. Six weapons. One murdered victim. But only one room holds the truth. Teams enter three staged crime scenes, the Study, Living Room, and Dining Room, where hidden details and forensic clues conceal the reality of what happened. With the moved-body twist already in play, investigators must use sharp observation and critical thinking to determine the true scene of death.

Alongside their investigation, teams must decode six cryptic clues to identify the weapons hidden within the crime. Some clues lie between the lines, while others hide in plain sight. Examine, question, connect, and record your findings before time runs out.

Five suspects. Five alibis. Countless lies. The investigation moves beyond the crime scene as five suspects enter the case, each carrying a motive, an alibi, and something to hide. But answers do not come freely. Teams must first hunt down and solve riddles scattered across campus to earn interrogation questions. Every question matters, and every answer could expose a contradiction.

Alongside their investigation, teams must decode six cryptic clues to identify the weapons hidden within the crime. Some clues lie between the lines, while others hide in plain sight. Examine, question, connect, and record your findings before time runs out.

Every clue has led here. Every lie must now be confronted. Teams must bring together the rooms, weapons,and testimonies leaks to reconstruct the crime and uncover the final truth. Build your case, challenge your own assumptions, and decide exactly what happened, where it happened, how it happened, and whether a culprit exists at all.

The investigation ends with a written case theory followed by a live reconstruction before the judges. Your evidence must speak, your reasoning must hold, and your story must withstand scrutiny. In the final moments, there is nowhere left to hide. The truth is yours to prove.

Delegates will dive into the world of pure sciences, where their understanding of chemistry, physics, and biology will be tested through challenges that demand sharp thinking, problem-solving, and creativity. Every round will count from how well they recall facts to how creatively they think their way out of a problem as only the most well-rounded scientists will make it to the top. Each stage will push them to apply scientific concepts in unexpected ways, blending knowledge with intuition as they compete to emerge as the true masters of Malpighi’s Manifestation.

The first round will put your core scientific knowledge to the test. This round will require teams to make an important strategic decision: when is it worth continuing with the difficult questions, and when is it better to move on and chase points elsewhere? Teams will begin with a challenging written assessment covering Physics, Chemistry, and Biology. The questions will range from demanding applications of concepts to problems requiring careful scientific reasoning, so simply memorising information will not be enough.

However, the round will not end with the test alone. Teams will also have the opportunity to engage in rapid-fire science trivia, providing a faster-paced way to accumulate additional points. These trivia challenges will focus on quick thinking, scientific recall, and basic application across different areas of science.
Only the strongest performers will advance.
Get ready to take science to the battlefield.

In this round, teams will face off directly against another team in a scientific battle of questions, decisions, and precision. The battlefield will take the form of a Battleshipstyle challenge, where teams will attempt to locate and strike their opponents' hidden positions. But every move will depend on their ability to answer scientific questions correctly.

Questions will draw from the Pure Sciences and Mathematics, requiring teams to think quickly and communicate effectively under pressure. A correct answer could give your team the opportunity to attack. A successful strike could open the door to another attack. This round will test not only what your team knows, but also how effectively you can perform when another team is standing directly across the battlefield.
You can try to figure it out beforehand. We wouldn't recommend it. Some things are better discovered than explained.
A major corporation stands accused of causing serious, documented environmental harm. The case has reached the courtroom.

Delegates will take on the roles of Prosecution and Defence, using real evidence, environmental science, and policy reasoning to establish what happened, assess who is responsible, determine the scale and significance of the damage, and defend an appropriate response.

Cases are drawn from real, publicly documented corporate environmental incidents, including oil spills, deforestation and land-clearing fires, industrial contamination, and mining disasters. The category goes beyond identifying environmental harm: delegates must connect cause to consequence, evidence to claim, and responsibility to remedy. They must distinguish established facts from assumptions, evaluate competing arguments fairly, and defend practical solutions under pressure.

Teams receive a case file containing the shared background, their Prosecution or Defence brief, and an evidence timeline. After preparation, each side delivers an opening statement outlining what happened, who it holds responsible, and what it intends to prove.

Teams then face cross-examination by the opposing side. Throughout the round, the judge may introduce a Judge’s Challenge, a new piece of context, a pointed question, or a difficult hypothetical, which both sides must address on the spot.
Judged on: evidence accuracy, clarity and structure, strength of argument and rebuttal, environmental reasoning, and the ability to adapt under pressure while maintaining a coherent case.

Roles from Round 1 do not carry over. All teams receive a new real-world environmental crisis and must respond through a crisis simulation, where evolving updates may change the situation and force teams to revise their strategy.

Teams then present and defend their response, explaining its scientific basis, feasibility, environmental impact, and resource requirements. Judges will assess the strength, practicality, innovation, and adaptability of each proposal before allocating funding.
Teams must not only manage the crisis effectively, but also convince the judges that their solution deserves the resources required to implement it.
Delegates should have a working understanding of:
Reading environmental graphs, maps, tables & scientific evidence

Each team will be allocated 5 scripts belonging to 5 randomized fandoms. Each script will contain 10 errors in it's wording, format, timestamp or line number. Delegates will need to circle the mistakes present in the scripts.

However, there's a catch! Each team will be given one "Choice Card", which they can use at the beginning to switch out one of their scripts for another script from the pool of 10 scripts, excluding the scripts the teams already have.

There will be a total of 30 minutes allotted to teams to circle all the 50 mistakes present in the scripts. Use of external devices such as phones, laptops, and tablets are strictly prohibited and may lead to diqualification from the category.
This is not a knockout round but will be worth 20% overall.

Teams will get to pick a fandom from a list and then will be tasked to bring it to life. Materials included in the list will be provided to the delegates to make relevant props for their reenactment if they wish to do so. Delegates will be required to deliver a 60-90 second performance for the scene they had chosen to reenact.
This will be a knockout round and will account for 30% of the total score.
The teams with the two highest scores will be crowned winner and runner up. Do you think you have what it takes? Come find out!

Delegates will engage in a series of robotics and engineering challenges designed to test their technical skills, creativity, and teamwork. Across multiple rounds, they will code, build, and strategize. Performance in each stage will determine their overall standing in the competition.
Participants are required to bring pre-built robots to this round and ensure that their robots comply with the technical and operational guidelines.
Robots will be inspected by the judges to ensure that they meet the required criteria. Once approved, teams will be allowed to practice on the provided track.
Teams will also have the opportunity to build their robots at school for an additional cost.

Note: Teams that choose to build their robots at school must inform the category heads. Delegates must only bring the components required for building their robots. Ingenium will provide only the basic tools required for assembly. Time allowed: 3 Hours
The best completion time for each team will be recorded on the given line-following track.
Each team will be invited to run their robot on the track, and their fastest completion time will be recorded. The top three teams will receive a hidden advantage in the next round.
Delegate cap: 3-5 delegates Time allowed: 2 Hours
The final showdown where the delegates will battle it out for glory. The exact bracket format will be announced at a later date.
Time allowed: 2 Hours Match Duration: 10 minutes per match

1. Arduino-based microcontroller. 2. Any motor driver except the IBT-2 motor driver. 3. Any geared DC motor, except high-end series such as the 775. 4. Caster wheel (optional). 5. Plywood or acrylic chassis (custom-built chassis are allowed; metal and 3D-printed chassis are not allowed). 6. Li-Po batteries are not allowed. Only one battery pack may be used to power the entire system, with a maximum voltage of 13V. 7. Any IR sensor, such as LM393, BFD1000, QTR-8, or TCRT5000. 8. HC-05 Bluetooth module. 9. Wires of all types (male-to-male, female-to-female, and male-to-female).
Participants may design and use an actuator for their sumo robot.
Small motors: Maximum of 2, such as MG90-series motors.
Heavy motors: Maximum of 1, such as the MG995R.
A lifting mechanism is allowed, subject to the rules specified in the rulebook.
Use only the provided kit components given in the list.
Teams may write/upload their own Arduino code.
Teams must bring their own laptop + Arduino IDE for coding.
Teams are allowed to use lifting/linear push mechanisms for Sumo Wars but mechanisms like pinching/high-velocity strikes are not allowed.
Adjustments using tape, glue, or cardboard reinforcements are permitted (non-electrical).
External sensors, motors, or custom hardware beyond the specifications of the component list.
High power external batteries not approved by organizers.
Any attempt to damage another team’s robot intentionally outside the rules of Sumo Wars.
Dimension of the robot exceeding 1 feet x 1 feet.

Teams will be given a random STEM-based concept, phenomenon, problem, or discovery and will transform it into a visual artwork. The concept may come from Physics, Biology, Chemistr, or other STEM fields The artwork does not need to be a literal representation. Teams may use abstract, symbolic, conceptual, or metaphorical interpretations to communicate the assigned idea.
Teams will create an artwork based on their assigned
The artwork should communicate the meaning, idea, or effect of the concept through visual elements rather than simply illustrating its scientific definition
Materials: A4 drawing sheets will be provided. Participants will use their own art materials. Any medium except oil paints

One member from each team will be randomly selected and given a STEM-related object, concept, or idea to draw. The selected member must communicate the prompt through drawing while their team attempts to guess it.
No writing or spelling the answer.
Teams must guess within the given time.
Successful guesses will earn bonus point.
Teams will transform a given STEM concept into a short live theatrical performance. Each team will receive three elements:
A scientific concept that must play an important role in the story
A setting or scenario in which the performance must take place.
No writing or spelling the answer.
Teams must guess within the given time.
Successful guesses will earn bonus point.
A restriction that must be followed throughout the performance
A specific word cannot be used.
The entire scene must be performed in slow motion.
Teams must combine all three elements into one coherent performance, with the STEM concept being an important part of the actual story rather than simply being mentioned or explained.
teams will receive a surprise STEM-related development that they were not given beforehand.
"You have travelled 100 years into the future."
Teams must immediately incorporate the new development into their performance without stopping, restarting, or breaking character.
All three assigned elements must be incorporated.
The STEM concept must directly influence the story or events.
The theatrical restriction must be followed.
The surprise twist must be incorporated immediately (bonus points).
Teams may not stop or restart after receiving the twist.
Performances must remain within the allotted time.
Teams will create a short film inspired by a given STEM concept. The assigned concept will act as the core idea, metaphor, or mechanism shaping the story.

The film does not need to directly explain or scientifically demonstrate the concept. Instead, teams should explore how the idea can be translated into a human story involving themes such as choices, relationships, identity, memory, loss, uncertainty, or perception
A character experiences two possible versions of their life simultaneously, with each version developing differently based on a different choice they made.
The assigned STEM concept must be central to the film.
The concept may be used literally, symbolically, or metaphorically.
The film must have a clear narrative or central idea.
Teams should focus on storytelling rather than explaining the science.
The scientific concept should influence the characters, events, setting, or conflict.
The film must be created and edited within the allotted time.

Somewhere between the letters, a message is waiting. Every cipher is a wall, and every wall has a crack. Vigenère's Veil is three rounds of finding it before the team next to you does. Think fast, work together, and keep your head when the clock gets louder than your own doubt.
This is not a category for the unprepared. Study the ciphers below. Know them cold.
This category consists of 3 rounds, held across the three days of the event.
The decisions of the organisers are final.
All rules outlined below are preliminary and may be adjusted before the event.

Your team moves as one chain, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Each delegate cracks their piece and passes it forward: decrypt, extract, hand off, then the next runner takes it from there. There's no time to double back. What you solve is what the next person has to work with, and what they solve decides how far your team gets. Speed matters. So does not breaking the chain.

Locked doors don't open for the slow. Somewhere in this room is a way out, but the path there won't be handed to you. Every step forward has to be earned, and not everything you need is written in plain sight. Some of it you'll have to find yourselves, and know where to look before you can even begin. The clock doesn't wait for teams that hesitate. Neither does the room.

The final stage is a duel: two teams, two hidden codes, one board between them. This round is built on the boardgame Mastermind. Every code you crack earns you the right to guess at your rival's, and every guess narrows the net a little further. Come knowing the game, not just the ciphers. The teams who've thought through their strategy in advance will have the edge once the board is in front of them.
Atbash · Caesar · Vigenère · Playfair (I/J share a cell) · ADFGVX · Rail Fence · Route Cipher (spiral inward, clockwise) · Pigpen · Templar · Hexadecimal / Binary
